messages.tutorial.window.title: NodeQL Workshop
messages.tutorial.window.subtitle: Isolated learning area · real nodes · live SQLite
messages.tutorial.window.emptyTitle: Choose a learning path to begin
messages.tutorial.window.emptyBody: This learning area is isolated from your projects. All nodes created here belong only to the current workshop session.
messages.tutorial.overview.title: Choose a practical learning path
messages.tutorial.overview.body: Eight SQLite workshops, two NodeQL-specific modules and {missions} hands-on missions. Learn each command with real nodes and an isolated practice database.
messages.tutorial.overview.datasetBody: Customers, orders and archived customers contain realistic practice data. The database is isolated from your projects, supports safe write exercises and is reset when you leave the workshop.
messages.tutorial.overview.allDone: Workshop complete — repeat any lesson whenever you like.
messages.tutorial.lesson.beginner.description: A guided 15-minute Simple Mode course: understand node shapes, labels, value reporters and a complete SELECT query.
messages.tutorial.lesson.beginnerSyntax.descripti: Build SQL syntax clause by clause: FROM, WHERE, AND, OR, ORDER BY and LIMIT, then solve a fresh query challenge.
messages.tutorial.lesson.intermediate.description: Join two tables, group records, use COUNT, filter groups and deliver a working report from scratch.
messages.tutorial.lesson.expert.description: Explore UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT and UNION ALL, then design and run an independent set-operation query.
messages.tutorial.lesson.selectAndSimpleFilters.d: Start with SELECT and narrow rows with a simple WHERE condition.
messages.tutorial.lesson.dataTypes.description: Use SQLite storage classes: NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT and BLOB.
messages.tutorial.lesson.advancedFilters.descript: Combine conditions with AND, OR and advanced comparison operators.
messages.tutorial.lesson.sortingAndWhere.descript: Filter, sort with ORDER BY and limit predictable result sets.
messages.tutorial.lesson.complexQueries.descripti: Build joins, aggregates, grouped reports and set operations.
messages.tutorial.lesson.dataManipulation.descrip: Safely add, change and remove records with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
messages.tutorial.lesson.schemaObjects.descriptio: Create tables, indexes and views and understand their roles.
messages.tutorial.lesson.transactions.description: Protect multi-step changes with transactions, savepoints and rollback.
messages.tutorial.lesson.databaseTools.descriptio: Learn NodeQL's database browser, SQLite editor, result pane and diagnostics.
messages.tutorial.lesson.plugins.description: Understand plugin shapes, permissions, repositories and safe extension use.
messages.tutorial.course.dataTypes.step.1.title: SQLite values use five storage classes
messages.tutorial.course.dataTypes.step.1.body: NULL represents no value, INTEGER stores whole numbers, REAL stores floating-point values, TEXT stores strings and BLOB stores bytes. NodeQL's Data Types palette creates correctly quoted literals for each class.
messages.tutorial.course.sortingAndWhere.step.1.t: Filter before you sort and limit
messages.tutorial.course.sortingAndWhere.step.1.b: WHERE decides which rows remain, ORDER BY makes their order deterministic and LIMIT reduces the final result. The visual chain follows the same order as the generated SQLite.
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change rows
INSERT adds records, UPDATE changes matching records and DELETE removes matching records. Always make the target table and WHERE condition explicit before running a write command.
messages.tutorial.course.schemaObjects.step.1.tit: Tables store data; indexes and views shape access
messages.tutorial.course.schemaObjects.step.1.bod: CREATE TABLE defines columns and constraints. CREATE INDEX can accelerate lookups, while CREATE VIEW gives a reusable name to a query without copying its rows.
messages.tutorial.course.transactions.step.1.body: BEGIN starts a transaction and COMMIT makes it permanent. SAVEPOINT marks a recovery point; ROLLBACK TO undoes only the work after it, and RELEASE closes the savepoint.
messages.tutorial.course.databaseTools.step.1.tit: Inspect, write, run and diagnose SQLite
messages.tutorial.course.databaseTools.step.1.bod: Use the database browser for tables and views, the SQLite editor for direct commands, the generated SQL preview to inspect node output and the result pane for rows and errors.
messages.tutorial.course.plugins.step.1.title: Plugin shape defines where a block belongs
messages.tutorial.course.plugins.step.1.body: Statement plugins join command chains, value plugins fit into rounded value slots and container plugins hold nested blocks. Read the declared inputs before connecting a plugin.
messages.tutorial.course.plugins.step.2.title: Review permissions and data access
messages.tutorial.course.plugins.step.2.body: A plugin manifest declares host requirements, network access and data sources. Install plugins only from repositories you trust and review those boundaries before using them with important databases.
messages.tutorial.course.plugins.step.3.title: Keep generated SQLite and plugin behavior inspectable
messages.tutorial.course.plugins.step.3.body: Reload the plugin directory after installation, find new blocks in the Plugins palette and inspect their generated SQLite or declared action before running a workflow.
messages.tutorial.practice.success: Solved — this workspace contains the required connected nodes.
messages.tutorial.practice.otherTab: The exercise is in another query tab.
messages.tutorial.practice.incomplete: The node chain is not complete yet. Use the checklist or reveal a hint.
messages.tutorial.practice.selectAndSimpleFilters: Connect SELECT and choose columns plus the customers table.
Drag SELECT below EXECUTE QUERY and replace placeholder values.
SELECT chooses the values returned by a query and FROM identifies their source.
Connect WHERE and configure one complete comparison.
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Berlin';
WHERE removes rows that do not satisfy its predicate.
Build SELECT and WHERE from scratch, then run the generated SQLite.
Use customers and a real column such as country or active.
SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE country = 'DE';
A useful query combines a clear result shape with an intentional row filter.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.1.title: Return a typed literal
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.1.instr: Insert a Data Type value node into SELECT and configure its value.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.1.hint: Open Data Types and try INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB or NULL.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.1.conce: SQLite values use NULL, INTEGER, REAL, TEXT or BLOB storage classes.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.2.title: Compare with a TEXT value
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.2.instr: Place a TEXT reporter in WHERE's value slot.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.2.hint: Set the TEXT value to Berlin and compare it with city.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.2.examp: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Berlin';
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.2.conce: Typed reporters let NodeQL quote text while leaving numeric values unquoted.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.3.title: Project: execute a typed SELECT
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.3.instr: Inspect the prepared typed literal and run it successfully.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.3.hint: The TEXT reporter must remain inserted in SELECT.
messages.tutorial.practice.dataTypes.step.3.conce: The generated SQL shows exactly how a typed NodeQL value reaches SQLite.
messages.tutorial.practice.advancedFilters.step.1: Add a configured AND condition after WHERE.
AND keeps a row only when both conditions are true.
messages.tutorial.practice.advancedFilters.step.2: Add a configured OR condition after the existing filter.
Try country = FR as an alternative.
… WHERE city = 'Berlin' AND active = 1 OR country = 'FR';
OR accepts rows that satisfy either side; remember SQLite's operator precedence.
messages.tutorial.practice.advancedFilters.step.3: Build and execute a SELECT with WHERE, AND and OR.
Configure every comparison and keep WHERE before AND and OR.
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE country = 'DE' AND active = 1 OR city = 'Paris';
Compound predicates express precise inclusion rules for result rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.sortingAndWhere.step.1: Add ORDER BY with a column and ASC or DESC direction.
Sort by name ASC after WHERE.
… WHERE city = 'Berlin' ORDER BY name ASC;
ORDER BY makes result order explicit and repeatable.
messages.tutorial.practice.sortingAndWhere.step.2: Connect LIMIT after ORDER BY and enter a positive row count.
LIMIT is predictable when it is applied after an explicit sort.
messages.tutorial.practice.sortingAndWhere.step.3: Build and execute WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT in a complete SELECT.
Use a real filter, sort column and positive limit.
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 5;
Filtering, sorting and limiting form the basis of search results and pages.
Connect a JOIN and configure its table and matching columns.
… FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id;
JOIN combines related rows through a deliberate key relationship.
Add configured GROUP BY and HAVING nodes in that order.
Group by customers.name and use HAVING COUNT(*) > 0.
GROUP BY forms groups; HAVING filters the calculated groups.
Connect UNION and enter a complete compatible SELECT.
Use SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers.
SELECT id, name FROM customers UNION SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers;
UNION combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate rows.
Build a JOIN with COUNT, GROUP BY and HAVING, then execute it.
Count orders per customer and keep groups with at least one order.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id GROUP BY customers.name HAVING COUNT(*) > 0;
Complex queries stay understandable when relationship, aggregation and group filter remain visible.
Insert a row
Connect INSERT and configure a table, columns and values.
Use archived_customers with id, name and a matching value tuple.
INSERT INTO archived_customers (id, name) VALUES (999, 'Workshop');
INSERT creates rows; its value count must match the selected columns.
Update matching rows
Connect UPDATE and configure its assignment plus WHERE comparison.
Target archived_customers and identify a row by id.
UPDATE archived_customers SET name = 'NodeQL' WHERE id = 999;
UPDATE without a precise WHERE can change more rows than intended.
Delete matching rows
Connect DELETE and configure a precise WHERE comparison.
Delete one archived customer by id.
DELETE FROM archived_customers WHERE id = 999;
DELETE removes every row matching its predicate, so the condition is essential.
Project: complete a row lifecycle
Run the prepared INSERT → UPDATE → DELETE chain.
Inspect all three statements before running them together.
INSERT …; UPDATE … WHERE id = 999; DELETE … WHERE id = 999;
A lifecycle exercise shows how records are created, changed and removed safely.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.1.i: Connect CREATE TABLE and define a name plus columns.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.1.h: Try workshop_notes with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and note TEXT NOT NULL.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.1.e: CREATE TABLE workshop_notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT NOT NULL);
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.1.c: A table definition gives stored values names, types and constraints.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.2.i: Add CREATE INDEX for a real table and column.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.2.h: Index workshop_notes.note and give the index a unique name.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.2.c: Indexes trade storage and write work for faster lookups.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.3.i: Connect CREATE VIEW and provide its name plus a complete SELECT.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.3.h: Create active_customers from customers WHERE active = 1.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.3.e: CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE active = 1;
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.3.c: A view stores a reusable query, not a separate copy of its result rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.4.i: Run the prepared table, index and view definitions.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.4.h: IF NOT EXISTS makes this practice chain safe to repeat.
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.4.e: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS …; CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS …; CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS …;
messages.tutorial.practice.schemaObjects.step.4.c: Tables, indexes and views solve different storage and access concerns.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.1.in: Connect BEGIN TRANSACTION and COMMIT in that order.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.1.hi: Choose DEFERRED, IMMEDIATE or EXCLUSIVE for BEGIN.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.1.co: COMMIT makes all successful changes since BEGIN permanent together.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.2.in: Connect SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT and RELEASE with the same name.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.2.hi: Use workshop_point for all three nodes.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.2.ex: SAVEPOINT workshop_point; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT workshop_point; RELEASE SAVEPOINT workshop_point;
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.2.co: A savepoint lets part of a transaction be undone without abandoning the whole transaction.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.3.in: Run the prepared transaction and verify its recovery-point order.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.3.hi: The UPDATE is undone before the savepoint is released and the transaction commits.
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.3.ex: BEGIN; SAVEPOINT workshop_point; UPDATE …; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT workshop_point; RELEASE SAVEPOINT workshop_point; COMMIT;
messages.tutorial.practice.transactions.step.3.co: Recovery points make multi-step writes safer and easier to reason about.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.title: Practice: Build your first query
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.instruction: Drag a SELECT node below EXECUTE QUERY. Configure its columns and table directly on the node.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.hint: Find SELECT in the Query Language palette on the left and drag it to the highlighted connector below the starter node.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginnerSyntax.title: Practice: Add a row filter
messages.tutorial.practice.beginnerSyntax.instruc: Extend the prepared SELECT query with a WHERE node and configure column, operator and value.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginnerSyntax.hint: Place WHERE below SELECT. A simple condition such as id = 1 is enough.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.title: Practice: Join two tables
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.instructi: Insert a JOIN after FROM and configure the second table plus its key relationship.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.hint: Use INNER JOIN. Connect customers.id with orders.customer_id, or configure another complete ON condition.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.title: Practice: Filter aggregate groups
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.instruction: Extend the prepared query with GROUP BY followed by HAVING.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.hint: First group by customer_id, then add HAVING with an aggregate condition such as COUNT(*) > 0.
messages.tutorial.practice.modeHelp.simple: Simple Mode uses plain-language node labels. Watch the live SQLite preview to learn the syntax behind them.
messages.tutorial.practice.modeHelp.advanced: Advanced Mode mirrors SQLite keywords directly on the nodes and exposes every relevant field.

messages.tutorial.practice.node.eventGreenFlag.bo: This hat-shaped node is the root. Only nodes snapped below it belong to the executable query and count for a mission.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlSelect.title: SELECT · choose result columns
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlSelect.body: SELECT defines what the result contains. In the compact beginner node it can also hold the source table.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlColumn.title: COLUMN · value reporter
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlColumn.body: Rounded value nodes do not extend the vertical query chain. They plug into a matching input slot and provide a column expression.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlWhere.title: WHERE · filter rows
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlWhere.body: WHERE keeps only rows that satisfy a condition made from a column, comparison operator and value.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlText.title: TEXT · safe text value
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlText.body: TEXT is a rounded value node. Insert it into a value slot so NodeQL can represent and quote text separately from the condition.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlAnd.title: AND · require another condition
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlAnd.body: AND extends an existing WHERE filter. A row remains only when the first and the additional condition are both true.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlOrderBy.title: ORDER BY · sort the result
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlOrderBy.body: ORDER BY chooses the sort column. ASC sorts upward; DESC reverses the order.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlLimit.title: LIMIT · control result size
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlLimit.body: LIMIT belongs near the end of a query and returns only a positive maximum number of rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlFrom.title: FROM · choose a source table
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlFrom.body: FROM names the table that supplies rows. In Advanced Mode it is a separate clause below SELECT; in Simple Mode the source can also sit inside SELECT.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlOr.title: OR · allow an alternative
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlOr.body: OR keeps a row when at least one condition is true. Without parentheses, SQLite evaluates AND before OR, so check your logic in the live result.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlInnerJoin.body: An INNER JOIN matches rows from both tables using key columns, such as customers.id and orders.customer_id. Rows without a match disappear.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlJoin.title: JOIN · connect related tables
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlJoin.body: Choose a join type and match key columns, such as customers.id and orders.customer_id. INNER JOIN returns rows with a partner in both tables.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlGroupBy.title: GROUP BY · form groups
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlGroupBy.body: GROUP BY turns many rows into groups by a chosen column. Add an aggregate such as COUNT to summarize each group.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlHaving.title: HAVING · filter groups
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlHaving.body: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters the grouped results using an aggregate condition.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCount.title: COUNT · count matching rows
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCount.body: COUNT is a value reporter. Insert it into SELECT and use * to count rows in each group; it does not extend the vertical clause chain.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlUnion.title: UNION · combine result sets
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlUnion.body: UNION combines compatible SELECT results and removes duplicates. Both sides must return the same number of columns.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlIntersect.body: INTERSECT returns rows that occur in both SELECT results. Match their column counts and compatible values.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlExcept.title: EXCEPT · subtract rows
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlExcept.body: EXCEPT keeps rows from the first SELECT that are absent from the second SELECT result.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlInsert.title: INSERT · add rows
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlInsert.body: INSERT targets a table, names its columns and supplies one or more matching value tuples.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlUpdate.title: UPDATE · change rows
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlUpdate.body: UPDATE assigns a new value to matching rows. Its WHERE condition controls the affected scope.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlDelete.title: DELETE · remove rows
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlDelete.body: DELETE removes every row matching its WHERE condition. Review the predicate before execution.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCreateTable.bo: CREATE TABLE defines a table's columns, SQLite affinities and constraints.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCreateIndex.bo: CREATE INDEX builds a lookup structure for selected columns; it can speed reads while adding write cost.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCreateView.bod: CREATE VIEW gives a reusable name to a SELECT without copying its result rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlBeginTransacti: BEGIN starts an atomic unit of work and chooses when SQLite acquires its lock.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCommit.title: COMMIT · keep changes
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlCommit.body: COMMIT makes all successful changes in the current transaction permanent.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlSavepoint.body: SAVEPOINT creates a named recovery point inside a transaction.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlRollbackToSave: ROLLBACK TO undoes work performed after the named savepoint while keeping the transaction open.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlReleaseSavepoi: RELEASE removes the named savepoint after it is no longer needed.
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlAlias.title: ALIAS · name an expression
messages.tutorial.practice.node.sqlAlias.body: ALIAS wraps another value reporter, such as COLUMN, and gives the output column a useful name with AS.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.1.title: Connect your first SELECT
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.1.instru: Drag a SELECT node from Query Language onto the connector below EXECUTE QUERY. Set its table to customers.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.1.hint: The top notch of SELECT must snap into the lower connector of EXECUTE QUERY. A floating node does not count.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.1.concep: A query is a connected graph, not a pile of nodes. The start node marks the executable root; SELECT is the first statement in this learning path.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.2.title: Insert a COLUMN value node
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.2.instru: Drag COLUMN into the rounded columns input of the prepared SELECT and choose name.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.2.hint: COLUMN is a rounded reporter. Drop it inside SELECT's columns slot rather than below the query chain.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.2.concep: Statement nodes form the vertical query. Rounded reporter nodes provide values inside those statements. This distinction is central to NodeQL.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.3.title: Filter rows with WHERE
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.3.instru: Snap WHERE below SELECT. Choose city, the equals operator and Berlin as the comparison value.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.3.hint: WHERE belongs after SELECT. All three parts — column, operator and value — must describe a complete condition.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.3.exampl: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = 'Berlin';
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.3.concep: SQLite processes WHERE as a row filter. Rows that do not make the condition true are removed before the result is shown.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.4.title: Use TEXT as an inserted value
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.4.instru: Replace WHERE's direct value with a TEXT reporter and enter Berlin in that inserted node.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.4.hint: Drag TEXT from SQLite data types into WHERE's rounded value input. The reporter must contain non-empty text.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.4.concep: Separating a literal value into its own node makes data types visible. NodeQL can then render text correctly while the WHERE node keeps the comparison structure.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.5.title: Add a second rule with AND
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.5.instru: Snap AND below WHERE and configure another complete condition, for example active = 1.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.5.hint: AND cannot start a filter by itself. It extends the WHERE condition and therefore belongs below it.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.5.concep: AND combines conditions strictly: both must be true. It is different from OR, where either condition may be true.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.6.title: Sort the matching rows
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.6.instru: Connect ORDER BY after the filters. Choose name and a valid ascending or descending direction.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.6.hint: Use name with ASC to sort alphabetically from A to Z. ORDER BY belongs after WHERE and AND.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.6.concep: A database does not promise a natural row order. ORDER BY makes the result deterministic for people and later processing.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.7.title: Finish with LIMIT
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.7.instru: Snap LIMIT below ORDER BY and enter a positive row count such as 5.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.7.hint: LIMIT is the final node in this query. Zero and negative values do not satisfy the mission.
messages.tutorial.practice.beginner.step.7.concep: LIMIT reduces how many sorted rows SQLite returns. This is useful for previews, pages and keeping large results manageable.
Build SELECT and FROM as separate nodes
A SELECT node is prepared. Connect FROM below it and choose customers as its source table.
FROM belongs immediately after SELECT when the source is represented by its own node.
Connect WHERE after FROM and configure column, comparison operator and value.
Use country = DE. The live preview shows how NodeQL quotes text for SQLite.
Add an AND node after WHERE and configure a second condition yourself.
WHERE starts the filter; AND can only extend it afterwards. Try city = Berlin.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.1.in: Connect a JOIN after FROM. Set the second table and connect customers.id to orders.customer_id.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.1.hi: INNER JOIN is a good default. Both key fields and the joined table must be configured.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.1.ex: … FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id;
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.2.in: Add GROUP BY after the JOIN and choose the column that defines each group.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.2.hi: Group by customers.name so one result group is produced per customer.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.3.in: Connect HAVING after GROUP BY and configure an aggregate condition.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.3.hi: HAVING filters groups rather than individual rows. COUNT(*) > 0 is a valid example.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.1.title: Combine two result sets
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.1.instruct: Connect UNION to the prepared SELECT and enter a compatible second SELECT statement.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.1.hint: Both SELECT statements should return the same number of columns, for example id and name.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.1.example: SELECT id, name FROM customers UNION SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers;
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.2.title: Sort the combined result
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.2.instruct: Connect ORDER BY after UNION and choose a result column and direction.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.2.hint: Sorting belongs after the set operation. Try name ascending.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.3.title: Limit the final result set
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.3.instruct: Finish the chain with LIMIT and configure how many combined rows SQLite should return.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.3.hint: LIMIT is the final clause. Connect it below ORDER BY and enter a positive row count.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.3.example: … UNION … ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 10;
SELECT chooses columns; FROM names the source table. Connecting them vertically mirrors the order of a written SQLite query.
A predicate compares a column with a value. Text values need quoting in generated SQL, while the node editor lets you focus on the condition.
AND narrows the result: both conditions must be true. Compare the live SQL with the node order before continuing.
Connect OR after your filter and configure another complete condition, such as city = Berlin. Then run the query and notice how the result widens.
OR is in Query Language. It needs a column, operator and value, and must be connected after WHERE.
… WHERE country = 'DE' AND active = 1 OR city = 'Berlin';
OR admits a row when either side is true. SQLite evaluates AND before OR; use parentheses in advanced SQL when another grouping is intended.
Add ORDER BY after the filters. Sort by name in ASC or DESC direction and compare the result with the unsorted output.
ORDER BY belongs below the WHERE/AND/OR chain. Choose a real result column and ASC or DESC.
SQLite does not guarantee row order without ORDER BY. A sort direction makes the final order predictable.
Connect LIMIT after ORDER BY and choose a positive row count. Run the query to see the preview shrink.
LIMIT comes last. Enter a whole number above zero, for example 5.
LIMIT acts after sorting. Sorting first ensures you know which rows make it into a small preview.
On a fresh canvas, connect SELECT → FROM → WHERE → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Use customers, configure every clause, then run the generated SQL successfully.
Start with SELECT and FROM. Add a complete WHERE condition such as active = 1, sort by name and limit the result to 5 rows.
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE active = 1 ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 5;
This independent project checks the whole query flow. A node graph is only useful when the generated SQLite also executes on real data.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.1.co: A JOIN relates rows using matching keys. Here customers.id identifies the person, while orders.customer_id points back to that person.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.2.co: GROUP BY forms one group per chosen customer. Without an aggregate in SELECT, the grouping is harder to read; you will add one next.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.3.co: WHERE filters before grouping; HAVING filters afterwards. COUNT(*) > 0 retains groups with at least one joined order.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.4.in: Insert a COUNT value reporter into SELECT's columns slot and configure it to count rows. Keep the JOIN and GROUP BY chain connected.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.4.hi: COUNT is rounded. Drop it inside SELECT, not underneath HAVING. Use * to count every row in each group.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.4.ex: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id GROUP BY customers.name;
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.4.co: An aggregate reporter turns each group into a summary value. COUNT(*) counts joined rows, so customers with more orders receive higher counts.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.5.in: Place ORDER BY after HAVING and choose a valid column and direction. Run the report to inspect the sorted groups.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.5.hi: Use customers.name ASC for an alphabetical report. ORDER BY follows HAVING, not the JOIN.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.5.ex: … GROUP BY customers.name HAVING COUNT(*) > 0 ORDER BY customers.name ASC;
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.5.co: Sorting grouped output makes a report reproducible. It occurs after the group filter.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.6.in: Add LIMIT below ORDER BY and set a positive count. Compare the rows before and after running the query.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.6.hi: LIMIT must follow ORDER BY and contain a number greater than zero.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.6.co: A report often needs only its first few rows. Always pair LIMIT with ORDER BY when which rows appear matters.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.7.in: Starting from SELECT and FROM, add a configured JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Insert an aggregate reporter into SELECT and run the finished SQL.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.7.hi: Join customers.id to orders.customer_id, group by customers.name, use COUNT(*) in SELECT, filter groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 0, then sort and limit.
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.7.ex: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers INNER JOIN orders ON customers.id = orders.customer_id GROUP BY customers.name HAVING COUNT(*) > 0 ORDER BY customers.name ASC LIMIT 5;
messages.tutorial.practice.intermediate.step.7.co: This project combines relationships, aggregation and presentation. The solution is checked as a connected graph and as an executable SQLite query.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.1.concept: UNION combines two SELECT results and removes duplicates. The columns must line up in number and meaning.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.2.concept: Sorting a set operation belongs after the second SELECT. It orders the combined result, not only one branch.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.3.concept: LIMIT after UNION and ORDER BY restricts the final combined result. Changing this order changes the question being asked.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.4.title: Keep rows shared by both sets
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.4.instruct: On a fresh prepared SELECT, connect INTERSECT and add SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers as its second query. Run it to find the shared record.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.4.hint: INTERSECT needs a complete second SELECT. The sample data contains Ada in both customer tables.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.4.example: SELECT id, name FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers;
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.4.concept: INTERSECT is the overlap of two results. Both branches must return compatible columns; the output contains only shared rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.5.title: Subtract archived records
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.5.instruct: On a fresh SELECT, connect EXCEPT and enter a complete SELECT against archived_customers. Run it to see which current rows remain.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.5.hint: Use SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers in EXCEPT's query field. Compare the result with INTERSECT.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.5.example: SELECT id, name FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers;
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.5.concept: EXCEPT subtracts the second set from the first. It is useful for finding records missing from a comparison set.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.6.title: Preserve duplicates with UNION ALL
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.6.instruct: Connect UNION to the fresh SELECT, configure a second SELECT and switch it to ALL. Run it and compare duplicate rows with plain UNION.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.6.hint: Use archived_customers as the second table and enable ALL in the UNION node. Ada should appear twice.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.6.example: SELECT id, name FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers;
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.6.concept: UNION removes duplicates, while UNION ALL retains them. ALL is often faster when duplicate removal is unnecessary.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.7.title: Choose unique values with DISTINCT
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.7.instruct: On a fresh SELECT from customers, switch SELECT to DISTINCT. Run the query and compare the unique values with the original rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.7.hint: The SELECT node has an ALL/DISTINCT choice. Set DISTINCT; use country as the result column for a compact comparison.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.7.concept: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows within one SELECT. Unlike UNION, it does not combine two different queries.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.8.title: Name a computed result with ALIAS
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.8.instruct: Insert an ALIAS reporter into SELECT's columns slot. Give it a real value, such as a COLUMN reporter for country, and a readable alias.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.8.hint: ALIAS is a rounded value node. Put COLUMN inside its value input and enter an alias such as region.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.8.example: SELECT DISTINCT country AS region FROM customers;
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.8.concept: AS changes the result column's displayed name without changing source data. An ALIAS reporter can wrap another reporter, showing nested node composition.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.9.title: Project: publish a combined result
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.9.instruct: Build SELECT, UNION, ORDER BY and LIMIT from a fresh root. Configure a compatible second SELECT, run SQLite and inspect the combined rows.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.9.hint: Use SELECT id, name FROM customers, UNION SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers, then ORDER BY name ASC and LIMIT 10.
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.9.example: SELECT id, name FROM customers UNION SELECT id, name FROM archived_customers ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 10;
messages.tutorial.practice.expert.step.9.concept: This final project checks compatible set branches, clause order and successful execution. A polished result is reproducible and easy to inspect.
messages.tutorial.solveFirst: Solve the short exercise to continue.
messages.tutorial.visual.runHint: NodeQL compiles your connected blocks into SQLite.
messages.tutorial.visual.errorHint: Syntax error near COUNT: check the selected columns.
messages.tutorial.visual.syntaxReady: You now know how NodeQL nodes map to SQLite syntax.
messages.tutorial.visual.ready: You are ready to build your first visual query.
messages.tutorial.step.1.title: Build SQLite without losing sight of SQLite
messages.tutorial.step.1.body: NodeQL combines visual blocks with real SQLite output. You can learn query structure, experiment locally and inspect every generated statement.
messages.tutorial.step.2.title: Three areas, one workflow
messages.tutorial.step.2.body: Choose blocks on the left, assemble them in the center and inspect SQLite plus database results on the right.
messages.tutorial.step.2.question: Where do you assemble a query?
messages.tutorial.step.3.title: Read the blocks from top to bottom
messages.tutorial.step.3.body: A query begins below EXECUTE QUERY. SELECT chooses data, FROM chooses its source and WHERE filters the rows.
messages.tutorial.step.3.question: Which block chooses the table?
messages.tutorial.step.4.title: Shapes reveal valid connections
messages.tutorial.step.4.body: Drag a block near a compatible connector. NodeQL highlights valid targets and preserves the logical SQLite order.
messages.tutorial.step.4.question: What should you do when no connector is highlighted?
messages.tutorial.step.4.answer.3: Move it to a compatible position
messages.tutorial.step.5.title: See the SQLite before it runs
messages.tutorial.step.5.body: Mount a local SQLite database, review the generated SQLite and select Run SQLite. Results and understandable errors appear in the lower output area.
messages.tutorial.step.5.question: Where can you verify the generated statement?
messages.tutorial.step.5.answer.2: In the SQLite output on the right
messages.tutorial.step.6.title: Plugin shapes communicate their role
messages.tutorial.step.6.body: Statement plugins join a chain, value plugins fit into value positions and container plugins hold nested blocks. Their extension rail identifies them at a glance.
messages.tutorial.step.6.question: Which plugin shape represents a reusable value?
messages.tutorial.step.7.title: A query needs a SQLite database
messages.tutorial.step.7.body: NodeQL works locally with SQLite files. Use Mount .db to choose a .db file. After that NodeQL knows tables and columns and can offer real names in dropdowns.
messages.tutorial.step.7.question: Why do you mount a .db file first?
messages.tutorial.step.7.answer.2: So tables and columns from the database are known
messages.tutorial.step.8.title: SELECT decides which columns you see
messages.tutorial.step.8.body: In the SELECT block you choose one or more columns. Everything means: show every column from the selected table. That is useful while learning; later individual columns are clearer.
messages.tutorial.step.8.question: What does SELECT do?
messages.tutorial.step.9.title: WHERE keeps only matching rows
messages.tutorial.step.9.body: A WHERE block has a column, an operator and a value. Example: film_id = 350. The database checks each row and keeps only rows where the condition is true.
messages.tutorial.step.9.question: Which three parts form a simple WHERE filter?
messages.tutorial.step.10.title: NodeQL explains every block as SQLite
messages.tutorial.step.10.body: The SQLite output is your checklist. Do table, columns and filters match your intention? If yes, run SQLite. If not, change the blocks.
messages.tutorial.step.10.question: Why should you inspect the SQLite output?
messages.tutorial.step.10.answer.2: You can see what the blocks mean before running them
messages.tutorial.step.11.title: Errors are hints, not dead ends
messages.tutorial.step.11.body: When SQLite fails, check the last change first. Often a table is missing, a column name is wrong or a value needs quotes. Change one block and test again.
messages.tutorial.step.12.title: Next comes the node and syntax tutorial
messages.tutorial.step.12.body: You now know the interface, database, SELECT, FROM, WHERE and SQLite output. Next you will learn the node types and how slots, reporters, joins, GROUP BY and HAVING work.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.1.title: Every node has a role in the query
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.1.body: NodeQL uses starter nodes, statement nodes and value nodes. Starter nodes begin execution, statement nodes form the SQLite chain and value nodes fill inputs inside other nodes.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.2.title: Statement nodes read like SQLite clauses
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.2.body: Blocks that stack vertically become the statement chain. Read them from top to bottom: SELECT describes the output, FROM chooses the table and later clauses refine the result.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.2.question: How do you read a statement chain in NodeQL?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.3.title: Slots are the editable parts of syntax
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.3.body: A slot is a placeholder inside a node. It can hold a column, text value, number, table name or reporter node, depending on what that SQLite clause expects.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.3.question: What does a slot inside a node represent?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.3.answer.3: An editable value in the SQLite syntax
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.4.title: Reporter nodes return a value
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.4.body: Reporter-style nodes fit into value slots. Examples are COUNT(*), UPPER(name), text literals and date functions. They do not run alone; they become part of a larger clause.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.4.question: Where does a reporter node belong?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.5.title: NodeQL protects the SQLite clause order
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.5.body: SQLite has a logical clause order. NodeQL helps preserve it: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE and GROUP BY appear in the positions where the database expects them.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.5.question: Which clause normally chooses the table source?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.6.title: Plugin nodes follow the same syntax rules
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.6.body: Plugin nodes can be statements, values or containers. Their shape tells you how they connect, and their declared inputs tell you which values are required.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.6.question: What tells you how a plugin node connects?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.7.title: SELECT and FROM form the smallest query
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.7.body: SELECT describes the output, FROM describes the source. In NodeQL both are visible as blocks. Once both are correct, the database knows what to show.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.7.question: Which two parts does a simple table query usually need?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.8.title: WHERE filters rows before output
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.8.body: WHERE runs before GROUP BY and before the final output. NodeQL splits the condition into column, operator and value so the check stays visible.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.8.question: When does WHERE apply?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.8.answer.3: When filtering individual rows before output
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.9.title: JOIN connects tables through matching columns
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.9.body: A JOIN needs a second table and two columns that belong together. In NodeQL you see this as left column = right column.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.9.question: What does the JOIN condition describe?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.10.title: GROUP BY creates groups, HAVING filters groups
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.10.body: GROUP BY summarizes rows by a column. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX calculate values over these groups. HAVING then checks conditions such as SUM(film_id) = 350.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.10.question: What does HAVING filter?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.11.title: ORDER BY sorts the finished result
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.11.body: ORDER BY does not change which rows exist. It only changes their order. Ascending means small to large or A to Z. Descending reverses that.
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.11.question: What does ORDER BY change?
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.12.title: Use nodes as readable SQLite pieces
messages.tutorial.syntax.step.12.body: When you add a node, ask what syntax role it plays: starter, statement, slot value, reporter or container. That habit makes NodeQL easier to learn and easier to debug.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.1.title: Build a complete readable query
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.1.body: Use the intermediate path when SELECT, FROM and WHERE already make sense. You will connect filters, joins, groups and execution checks into one workflow.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.2.title: Join tables through matching keys
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.2.body: A JOIN adds rows from another table. Keep the source table clear, then connect the join block and define the columns that identify matching records.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.2.question: What does a JOIN need to combine two tables reliably?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.3.title: Summarize rows with GROUP BY
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.3.body: Aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM and AVG summarize rows. GROUP BY decides which rows belong together before the result is shown.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.3.question: Which part decides the buckets for an aggregate result?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.4.title: Keep reusable values separate
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.4.body: Parameter-style values make a query easier to review and reuse. Put changing values into value slots instead of hiding them inside long SQLite text.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.4.question: Why should changing values stay in visible value slots?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.4.answer.1: They are easier to review and replace
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.5.title: Read the SQLite before trusting it
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.5.body: Before running a larger query, scan the SQLite output. Check table names, join conditions, filters and grouping before you use the result.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.5.question: What should you verify before running a larger query?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.6.title: Use plugin blocks by their shape
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.6.body: Plugin blocks follow the same connection rules as built-in blocks. Their shape tells you whether they belong in a statement chain, a value slot or a container.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.6.question: Where does a value plugin belong?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.6.answer.2: On top of the title bar
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.7.title: Use error messages as signposts
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.7.body: When a query fails, compare the error with the SQLite output. Look for misspelled columns, missing tables, invalid join conditions or values without quotes.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.7.question: What should you inspect first when a query fails?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.7.answer.2: The error message and generated SQLite
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.8.title: Check aggregate, column, operator and value separately
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.8.body: HAVING is clearer when you think in parts: which function, which column, which comparison, which threshold. Example: SUM(film_id) = 350.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.8.question: Which parts make a clear HAVING block?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.9.title: Review plugin blocks before using them
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.9.body: Before adding plugins to a query, read their shape, inputs and description. A value plugin belongs in a slot, a statement plugin in the chain and a container plugin around other blocks.
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.9.question: What tells you where a plugin belongs?
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.10.title: Rebuild a report in small checks
messages.tutorial.intermediate.step.10.body: Pick a report you understand, rebuild it as blocks and compare the generated SQLite after each added part. This keeps mistakes visible while the query grows.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.1.title: Treat NodeQL as a visual query layer
messages.tutorial.expert.step.1.body: The advanced path focuses on how blocks, generated SQLite, plugin manifests and data-source boundaries fit together. Use it when you already know SQLite concepts.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.2.title: Choose joins for intent, not habit
messages.tutorial.expert.step.2.body: INNER, LEFT and other join types express different result guarantees. Select the join that matches the question before tuning columns or filters.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.2.question: What should drive the selected join type?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.3.title: Separate row filters from group filters
messages.tutorial.expert.step.3.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation. Keeping those roles separate prevents subtle report errors.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.3.question: Which clause filters aggregate groups?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.4.title: Use generated SQLite as the debugging contract
messages.tutorial.expert.step.4.body: When a result looks wrong, inspect the SQLite first. The generated statement is the common contract between the visual workspace, the runtime and the database.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.4.question: What is the first artifact to inspect when a complex query fails?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.5.title: Respect plugin boundaries
messages.tutorial.expert.step.5.body: A plugin declares its block shape, inputs, data access and host requirements. Review those boundaries before mixing plugin behavior into a query workflow.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.5.question: What should a plugin declare before it is trusted in a workflow?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.6.title: Design queries so assumptions stay visible
messages.tutorial.expert.step.6.body: Expose thresholds, dates and filters as explicit values. That makes reviews easier and reduces accidental changes hidden inside a long statement.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.6.question: Which values should stay visible for review?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.7.title: Review queries like small programs
messages.tutorial.expert.step.7.body: Complex block chains need reviews. Is the source correct? Are joins intentional? Are rows and groups filtered in the right place? Is the result reproducible?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.7.question: Which question belongs in a query review?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.7.answer.1: Are source, joins, filters and result intent clear?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.7.answer.2: Is the window decoration bright enough?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.7.answer.3: Is the project name very long?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.8.title: Separate local SQLite logic from plugin behavior
messages.tutorial.expert.step.8.body: Plugins extend NodeQL, but they remain external contracts. Check host requirements, data access and expected inputs before treating plugin results as part of an important query.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.8.question: Why should plugin boundaries stay visible?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.8.answer.2: So data access and inputs remain reviewable
messages.tutorial.expert.step.9.title: Keep assumptions visible and changeable
messages.tutorial.expert.step.9.body: Good NodeQL projects explain themselves: fixed thresholds stay in value slots, important filters are named and the SQLite output stays readable enough to discuss.
messages.tutorial.expert.step.9.question: What makes a query more maintainable?
messages.tutorial.expert.step.9.answer.3: Visible values, clear filters and readable SQLite
messages.tutorial.expert.step.10.title: Teach the workflow by making intent explicit
messages.tutorial.expert.step.10.body: For advanced work, keep every block chain explainable: source, relation, filter, grouping, output and extension boundary. That discipline makes projects easier for others to learn.
